news_title: FDA gives Franko Herbal Centre 14 days to recall diazepam-tainted mixture - Graphic Online
efet_title: FDA gives Franko Herbal Centre 14 days to recall diazepam-tainted mixture - Graphic Online
efet_body:
Featured
FDA gives Franko Herbal Centre 14 days to recall diazepam-tainted mixture
Mohammed Ali
Oct - 20 - 2026 , 13:06
2 minutes read
The Food and Drugs Authority (FDA) has given Franko Herbal Centre 14 days to recall Franko Herbal Mixture from the market after the FDA said laboratory tests found the product contained diazepam and paracetamol, which were not declared as ingredients.
In a product recall notice signed by the Chief Executive Officer and dated October 19, 2026, the FDA directed the public, retailers and distributors to report anyone still selling the mixture to the nearest FDA office.
The Authority said the manufacturing factory at Jacobu in the Ashanti Region had been closed down. It added that the recalled products would be safely disposed of.
It warned Franko Herbal Centre that failure to comply with the directives could attract further regulatory sanctions, including criminal prosecution.
The FDA said the action followed laboratory analysis of Franko Herbal Mixture, manufactured by Franko Herbal Centre at Jacobu. The product was registered as containing three herbal plants, Carica papaya, Alstonia boonei and Tetrapleura tetraptera.
The analysis, however, established that the mixture had been adulterated with diazepam and paracetamol.
The Authority advised the public against purchasing or consuming the product. It also urged retailers and distributors to comply with the recall directive and report anyone offering the mixture for sale to help remove it from the market.
The FDA described diazepam as a benzodiazepine and a prescription-only medicine used to treat anxiety disorders, acute alcohol withdrawal, muscle spasms and certain types of seizures.
It said paracetamol was an over-the-counter medicine used to relieve mild-to-moderate pain and fever.
According to the Authority, the presence of the two drugs in a herbal medicinal product poses serious health risks.
It explained that diazepam could interact with other medicines and increase the risk of severe sedation, respiratory depression, coma and death.
Long-term use or abuse of the drug could also affect the central nervous system, causing confusion, forgetfulness, dizziness, fatigue, nightmares, hallucinations, impaired judgement and seizures, the FDA said.
On paracetamol, the Authority warned that an overdose could cause severe liver damage and acute liver failure, which could be fatal without prompt treatment.
The FDA said the adulteration of herbal medicinal products was an offence under Section 111 of the Public Health Act, 2012 (Act 851), which prohibits the sale of adulterated herbal medicinal products.
It added that the law also prohibited the manufacture, labelling, packaging, sale or advertisement of herbal medicinal products in ways that were false, misleading or deceptive about their character, nature, quality, substance or composition.
The Authority stated that Franko Herbal Mixture “flouts all these requirements and more”.
It explained that the product was registered as a herbal medicinal product and, therefore, must not contain any other drug substance.

news_title: FDA recalls Franko Herbal Mixture over diazepam, paracetamol presence - CitiNewsroom.com
efet_title: FDA recalls Franko Herbal Mixture over diazepam, paracetamol presence - CitiNewsroom.com
efet_body:
The Food and Drugs Authority (FDA) has ordered Franko Herbal Centre to recall its Franko Herbal Mixture from the market within 14 days after laboratory analysis detected the presence of diazepam and paracetamol in the product.
FDA also closed down the company’s manufacturing facility at Jacobu in the Ashanti Region and warned that failure to comply with the directives could attract further regulatory sanctions, including criminal prosecution.
In a statement, the FDA said it would oversee the safe disposal of all recalled products to ensure their complete removal from circulation and protect public health.
The regulatory action follows laboratory analysis of Franko Herbal Mixture, which is registered with the Authority as a herbal medicinal product containing Carica papaya, Alstonei boonei and Tetrapleura tetraptera.
However, the analysis established that the product had been adulterated with diazepam, a prescription-only medicine, and paracetamol, a medication commonly used to relieve pain and reduce fever.
The FDA said the presence of the two pharmaceutical substances in a product registered strictly as a herbal medicine violated regulatory requirements and posed serious health and safety risks to consumers.
The FDA explained that diazepam belongs to a class of medicines known as benzodiazepines and is prescribed for conditions including anxiety disorders, acute alcohol withdrawal, muscle spasms and certain types of seizures.
While the medicine has legitimate medical uses, the FDA warned that its presence in an unapproved herbal formulation could expose consumers to potentially dangerous effects, particularly when taken alongside other medications.
The Authority said diazepam can interact with other medicines and increase the risk of severe sedation, respiratory depression, coma and death.
FDA also cautioned that prolonged use or abuse of the drug could interfere with the functioning of the central nervous system.
Possible effects include confusion, forgetfulness, dizziness, fatigue, nightmares, hallucinations, impaired judgement and seizures.
The Authority also raised concerns about the presence of paracetamol in the mixture, explaining that although the medicine is commonly used for the temporary relief of mild-to-moderate pain and fever, excessive intake can have serious consequences.
It said the risks associated with the two substances reinforced the need for consumers to avoid the product while the recall and enforcement measures were being implemented.

news_title: FDA shuts down new Arcan Bitters factory in Ashanti Region - CitiNewsroom.com
efet_title: FDA shuts down new Arcan Bitters factory in Ashanti Region - CitiNewsroom.com
efet_body:
Officers from the Food and Drugs Authority (FDA) in the Ashanti Region have closed down a factory belonging to Unni Associates Company Limited, manufacturers of Arcan Bitters.
This was after officials discovered that the owners were operating a new factory at Senfi in the Bekwai Municipality after their factory located at Parkoso in the Asokore Mampong Municipality was shut down in September this year.
The FDA ordered the recall of Arcan Bitters from the Ghanaian market after laboratory analysis found the presence of undeclared Sildenafil Citrate, a prescription medicine used to treat erectile dysfunction and pulmonary arterial hypertension.
The Authority subsequently closed down the factory, but the owners, unbeknownst to FDA officers, opened a new factory and proceeded with the manufacturing of the alcoholic drink.
According to the FDA, laboratory tests established that the product, which is registered as a food product with an alcohol content of 35%, had been adulterated with Sildenafil Citrate, a Phosphodiesterase Type 5 inhibitor.
Ashanti Regional Head of the Food and Drugs Authority, Dr. Ashraf Haruna, explained that the presence of the undeclared drug substance in the alcoholic beverage poses serious health and safety risks to consumers.
The FDA officers locked up the facility and pasted caution notices at the entrances.
The 23 barrels containing alcoholic content to be used for manufacturing, about 1,500 boxes containing the products, over 5,000 empty bottles, and other materials have been secured by the FDA after the facility was closed.
The Ashanti Regional Head of the FDA says his office is in touch with the police to get the owner of the facility arrested.
The FDA said Arcan Bitters appears to have violated these requirements, stressing that the product is registered as an alcoholic food product and therefore must not contain any drug substance.
The officers advised the public to refrain from purchasing and consuming the product.
